title: Analysis of the sample complexity for PAC-learning functions defined over quantum states
abstract: A fundamental question in PAC learning is determining the number of labeled examples required to learn a concept class to a desired accuracy and confidence. In classical learning theory, this quantity is characterized by the VC-dimension, while several quantum generalizations have established analogous results when examples are provided in quantum superposition. In this work, we study a distinct quantum PAC-learning model in which concepts are functions acting on quantum states. We demonstrate that the VC-dimension, although still relevant, fails to fully capture the sample complexity of this model. To further characterize this setting, we develop a new lower bound on the required number of samples and establish an upper bound when the states in the domain are linearly independent. Remarkably, this upper bound has a form similar to the classical PAC-learning bound. We further examine a setting in which the learner receives more informative data and show that the limitations of the VC-dimension persist in this extended model.
summary: This paper develops a theory to determine how many quantum examples are needed to reliably learn a function defined over quantum states. It proves that classical measures like VC-dimension fail in this setting, establishing new bounds dependent on state overlaps and linear independence. This advances the theoretical understanding of quantum machine learning complexity.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the sample complexity required for PAC-learning functions defined over quantum states, aiming to characterize this complexity beyond classical measures.
main_result: It demonstrates that the VC-dimension is insufficient to characterize the quantum sample complexity; instead, bounds involve parameters related to state overlaps and linear independence of the quantum states.
method: The analysis involves deriving rigorous lower and upper bounds on the required number of samples using concepts like the quantum Chernoff distance and relating the problem to classical learning theory via auxiliary concepts.
model_or_system: The model considers concept classes $C$ whose functions act on quantum states $|\psiangle$ within a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Learning occurs from examples provided as pairs $(|\phiangle, c(|\phiangle))$.
key_observables: Sample complexity ($	ext{t}(\epsilon, \delta)$), VC-dimension ($d$), and the minimum eigenvalue of the state overlap matrix ($\lambda_{\min}(G)$).
important_parameters: The fidelity/overlap parameter $F = \sup |\langle\psi|\psi'angle|^2$, and the error tolerance $\epsilon$ and confidence $\delta$.
main_assumptions: A key result (Theorem 2) assumes that the quantum states $\{|\psi_iangle\}$ are linearly independent.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates how a complexity measure $\Lambda_C(\alpha)$ is bounded by constants related to state overlaps, showing its relationship to classical bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the inadequacy of VC-dimension in the quantum setting, deriving specific lower and upper bounds using concepts like opposite pairs, and finally presenting a general bound for linearly independent states that resembles classical PAC-learning results.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental theoretical tools for quantifying learnability when the input data is inherently quantum mechanical, which is crucial for developing robust quantum machine learning protocols.
